seq.by: read by the normalizer as part of the DEDUP KEY, and load-bearing beyond that: `hasSeq` decides WHICH dedup rule applies — a seq-bearing frame gets the remembered key that closes an A,B,A replay, one without it keeps the adjacent-only rule so a legitimately repeated delta is not swallowed. CORRECTED after reading the code: the old note said "frame dedup/tally; no gap detection (ordered WS)" and both halves were wrong. `tallyFrame` does NOT include seq (its key is type/event/state), and gap detection EXISTS — but on the ENVELOPE `frame.seq` (frame-seq.ts, exposed as `missingTotal`), which is a different field from this one. What is genuinely absent is gap detection on the PAYLOAD seq, and it is stated HERE — deliberately not in the gap list, which is a mechanical recount of the manifest's `gap` fields and cannot hold a path that does not exist. Corrected after review: an earlier version of this note pointed at that list.

transport.by: server.ts sends it on every create, from the /talk-session body; convex/talk.ts asks for `webrtc`. CORRECTED after review: an earlier note called that "the only client-owned transport" — the contract also defines `provider-websocket` as a browser session. The single-transport reality is a CHOICE Atrium makes, not a property of the protocol, and the session parser downstream is shaped to that choice

voice.by: forwarded from the /talk-session request body, which convex/talk.ts builds from the CALLER's arguments (bounded to 60 chars) — a per-conversation preference, not instance configuration. Omitted when absent, so the gateway default applies

vadThreshold.by: forwarded from the /talk-session request body; convex/talk.ts sends it only when it is a finite number strictly between 0 and 1, so an out-of-range value silently becomes 'use the gateway default' rather than a rejected session

sessionKey.why: Atrium does not send it at create: server.ts builds the `talk.client.create` body from `transport` plus the optional voice and VAD threshold, and nothing else. The conversation is named at consult time instead, by `talk.client.toolCall.sessionKey` (the agent session key `buildSessionKey` produces). CORRECTED after review: an earlier note inferred from this that the gateway mints the session "unattached" and that sending the key twice would create two identities — neither is established here, and upstream's own client does send it on create. What this classification rests on is Atrium's behaviour, not a guess about the server's

provider.why: which realtime provider serves voice is gateway configuration; the capability Atrium exposes is a per-instance yes/no

model.why: the REALTIME model (ears and mouth) is a different axis from the agent model the chat's knob selects: the consult itself runs as a normal agent turn through talk.client.toolCall and uses the session's own settings

reasoningEffort.why: same axis as `model` — belongs to the realtime voice model, not to the agent turn the consult spawns

silenceDurationMs.why: finer voice-activity tuning than Atrium exposes; the UI offers the threshold alone, and sending a partial tuning set would silently override gateway defaults for the rest

prefixPaddingMs.why: same finer VAD tuning as silenceDurationMs

mode.why: the gateway's talk MODE selection. Atrium always creates a client-held session and leaves the mode at the gateway default; `transport` already states the one axis it chooses

brain.why: which component answers inside the realtime session; Atrium always routes the substance to an agent turn via toolCall, so the brain choice is not its call

clientSecret.by: forwarded as part of `{ok:true, session}` and PROJECTED by the consumer (convex/lib/talk.ts): REQUIRED non-empty, else the session is refused. A short-lived provider credential — it transits to the authenticated chat owner and is never logged or persisted

offerUrl.by: forwarded as part of `{ok:true, session}` and PROJECTED by the consumer (convex/lib/talk.ts): REQUIRED and must be https, because the browser posts its SDP offer there; a non-https value is refused outright

provider.by: forwarded as part of `{ok:true, session}` and PROJECTED by the consumer (convex/lib/talk.ts): descriptive, defaulted to "" when absent

transport.by: forwarded as part of `{ok:true, session}` and PROJECTED by the consumer (convex/lib/talk.ts): descriptive, defaulted to "" when absent

model.by: projected by convex/lib/talk.ts (null when absent) and then LOAD-BEARING: `buildCallUrl` (src/chat/talkSession.ts) appends it as a query parameter on the SDP calls endpoint, because the provider's WebRTC flow requires it — omitting it 500s on the real offer (live repro 2026-07-16). CORRECTED after review: an earlier note called it "descriptive", which would have made it look droppable

voice.by: forwarded as part of `{ok:true, session}` and PROJECTED by the consumer (convex/lib/talk.ts): descriptive, null when absent

expiresAt.note: projected by convex/lib/talk.ts and read by NOBODY. CORRECTED after review: the first note claimed the browser uses it to know when the credential dies. It does not — the UI discovers expiry only from an HTTP 401 on the SDP offer, which it surfaces as `talk_secret_expired`. So a person whose secret expires while they were deciding learns it by a failed connection instead of a session that never opened stale. The value is already on hand; nothing consumes it.

knownReaders.note: projected to the client and read by nobody downstream; expiry is discovered via HTTP 401 on the SDP offer

websocketUrl.why: belongs to the json-pcm websocket branch of the union, which the consumer never accepts: it requires an https `offerUrl`, so only the WebRTC SDP shape survives. Atrium asks for `webrtc` — a choice, not a protocol constraint

relaySessionId.why: gateway-relay branch: the relay id only matters when the GATEWAY carries the audio, which Atrium's browser-held session never asks for

roomUrl.why: managed-room branch — same exclusion as the relay branch: not the transport Atrium requests

offerHeaders.note: NOT projected and NOT sent. The contract lets a session require extra headers on the SDP offer POST; convex/lib/talk.ts drops them and `exchangeSdp` (src/chat/talkSession.ts) sends `Authorization` and `Content-Type` only. CORRECTED after review: this was classified `ignored` while its own note admitted the handshake would fail — a reason that names a breakage is a GAP, not a deliberate exclusion. Impact: a gateway or provider that starts requiring a header fails voice in the browser, at the SDP exchange, with a bare `sdp_<status>` and nothing pointing here.

initialMessage.why: a first utterance the session may carry. Atrium opens a voice session on an existing conversation and lets the person speak first; injecting a message would put words in the turn nobody said

sessionKey.by: server.ts sends `buildSessionKey(chat, agent, canonical)` — the AGENT session key, so a voice consult lands in the same session as a typed turn

callId.by: server.ts forwards the voice model's call id, which correlates the reply

args.by: server.ts forwards the consult arguments the voice model produced

relaySessionId.why: only meaningful when the GATEWAY relays the audio; Atrium's browser holds the session, so there is no relay id to quote

runId.by: server.ts requires a non-empty runId (else `talk_malformed`), claims the run and drives it through the same RunManager/normalizer pipeline as a typed turn

idempotencyKey.note: NOT read: server.ts requires `runId` from the result and discards the rest, so the `idempotencyKey` the gateway returns is dropped. CORRECTED TWICE after review — the first note claimed keeping it would make a retry safe (`TalkClientToolCallParams` is additionalProperties:false and declares no such field, so there is nowhere to send it back), and the second asserted what the key identifies inside the gateway, which nothing here establishes. The verifiable fact is the whole gap: the gateway hands back an identifier for this consult and Atrium keeps none of it, so whatever that identifier is good for, we cannot use it.

TalkEvent.why: the gateway's canonical Talk event envelope (`turn.started`, `tool.call`, …). Nothing in Atrium reads it. CORRECTED after review: an earlier note said the BROWSER consumes it directly off the transport — it does not. The browser's data channel carries the PROVIDER's own event shapes, and `parseTalkToolCall` (src/chat/talkSession.ts) recognises exactly two of them (`response.output_item.done` and `response.function_call_arguments.done`), ignoring everything else. The gateway envelope is a lane Atrium is not on at all: the substance of a consult reaches it as a normal agent run instead
